newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil '96 deficit nice surprise, still worrisome.
newsitem.headline: Brazil '96 deficit nice surprise, still worrisome.

text.p: Improved financial performances by states and municipal governments helped Brazil post a better-than-expected 1996 operational budget deficit, but economists said the figure was still worrisome.

The Central Bank reported Friday that its closely-watched operational deficit, which includes expenditures on interest payments for government securities, closed 1996 at 3.89 percent of gross domestic product, compared to forecasts of a 4.5 percent shortfall.

"This is better than the latest forecasts, but it is not a great advance because at the beginning of last year we were all expecting a 3.0 percent gap for 1996 and this number is closer to 4.0 percent," said Thomas Malaga, an economist at Brazilian retail bank Unibanco.
The operational deficit, which covers budgetary performances by local, state and federal governments, is the primary indicator used to measure Brazil's fiscal performance.
Economists were still scrambling on Friday to determine exactly how states and municipal governments managed to turn in such better-than-expected budget numbers.
Some speculated that debt rescheduling deals struck between a number of states and the federal government last year may have significantly reduced the states' debt servicing burdens.
Others pointed to the fact that real interest payments by federal, state and local governments fell markedly from November to December based on Central Bank methodology.

The bank uses inflation figures from January and December to determine the December inflation rate. Because January's IGP-DI inflation index came in at a higher-than-normal 1.58 percent, it substantially reduced real interest rates for the bank's December calculations, economists said.
Real interest rates are nominal interest rates minus inflation.

"Because of the methodology, they had a strong drop in real interest payments from November to December, which helped the operational result," said Matthew Taylor, an economist at Trend Analise in Brazil.
Economists noted that although the deficit was better-than-expected, the government must continue to regard improving fiscal performance as its key challenge in 1997.
"The deficit is still incompatible with long-term stabilization so it is very important that the government does something to reduce the deficit in the next two years," Unibanco's Malaga said.
